verses.text: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper.
The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife.
She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him of his leprosy.”
Someone went in, and told his lord, saying, “The maiden who is from the land of Israel said this.”
The king of Syria said, “Go now, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel.” He departed, and took with him ten talents  of silver, and six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of clothing.
He brought the letter to the king of Israel, saying, “Now when this letter has come to you, behold, I have sent Naaman my servant to you, that you may heal him of his leprosy.”

When the king of Israel had read the letter, he tore his clothes, and said, “Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends to me to heal a man of his leprosy? But please consider and see how he seeks a quarrel against me.”

It was so, when Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, that he sent to the king, saying, “Why have you torn your clothes? Let him come now to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel.”
So Naaman came with his horses and with his chariots, and stood at the door of the house of Elisha.
Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall come again to you, and you shall be clean.”

But Naaman was angry, and went away, and said, “Behold, I thought, ‘He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of Yahweh his God, and wave his hand over the place, and heal the leper.’
Aren’t Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Couldn’t I wash in them, and be clean?” So he turned and went away in a rage.

His servants came near, and spoke to him, and said, “My father, if the prophet had asked you do some great thing, wouldn’t you have done it? How much rather then, when he says to you, ‘Wash, and be clean?’”
Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.

He returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and came, and stood before him; and he said, “See now, I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel. Now therefore, please take a gift from your servant.”
But he said, “As Yahweh lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none.” He urged him to take it; but he refused.
Naaman said, “If not, then, please let two mules’ burden of earth be given to your servant; for your servant will from now on offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice to other gods, but to Yahweh.

In this thing may Yahweh pardon your servant: when my master goes into the house of Rimmon to worship there, and he leans on my hand, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon. When I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, may Yahweh pardon your servant in this thing.”
He said to him, “Go in peace.” So he departed from him a little way.

But Gehazi the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, “Behold, my master has spared this Naaman the Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought. As Yahweh lives, I will run after him, and take something from him.”
So Gehazi followed after Naaman. When Naaman saw one running after him, he came down from the chariot to meet him, and said, “Is all well?”

He said, “All is well. My master has sent me, saying, ‘Behold, even now two young men of the sons of the prophets have come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent  of silver and two changes of clothing.’”

Naaman said, “Be pleased to take two talents.” He urged him, and bound two talents of silver in two bags, with two changes of clothing, and laid them on two of his servants; and they carried them before him.
When he came to the hill, he took them from their hand, and stored them in the house. Then he let the men go, and they departed.
But he went in, and stood before his master. Elisha said to him, “Where did you come from, Gehazi?” He said, “Your servant went nowhere.”

He said to him, “Didn’t my heart go with you, when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and olive groves and vineyards, and sheep and cattle, and male servants and female servants?
Therefore the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and to your offspring  forever.” He went out from his presence a leper, as white as snow.

footnotes.content: Here's a picture of a man caught between two truths: mighty in the world's eyes, yet broken in ways no victory can heal. The Lord's grace works through him even while his body betrays him. I've learned that the deepest strength often arrives when we stop trusting our own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A small captive girl, displaced and serving in a foreign house, holds the key to a general's salvation. The Lord's messenger often arrives unannounced, in the humblest form. She didn't know she was sent—but she spoke what she knew.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even in captivity, she remembers Elisha, remembers God's power, remembers that healing is possible. There's courage in those words—not bitterness, but faith that the Lord still works. Her masters could have dismissed a slave's wish as foolish talk.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A servant speaks to his master, and the word travels up the chain of command. Small words can move great men when they carry the hope of the Lord. I've seen this in my own life—sometimes all it takes is someone willing to pass on what they heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver, gold, fine robes—Naaman brings his wealth to buy what money cannot purchase. It's the first and hardest step toward healing: admitting that all you own cannot fix what's broken. The Lord loves to work with someone who finally sees their poverty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The letter carries an impossible demand wrapped in courtesy. Naaman's master speaks as though Elisha were a servant to be summoned, not understanding that prophets answer to God alone. How often have I assumed the Lord works on my terms?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king of Israel tears his clothes in panic, thinking this is a trap—a test of his power he cannot pass. Fear speaks louder than faith. He doesn't think to send Naaman to Elisha; he sees only a trap.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha hears the king's despair and simply asks: Why have you torn your clothes? He doesn't panic or defend himself—he sees an opportunity. The man of God knows whose authority rests on him. There's a quiet confidence that comes from standing before the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Naaman arrives with all his grandeur—horses, chariots, a show of power. He comes expecting ceremony, expecting to be met with the honors due a general. But the Lord's healing doesn't run on the world's schedule.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A messenger, not Elisha himself. Seven dippings in a river, not a dramatic laying-on of hands. The Lord's word comes plain and simple, asking only for obedience. How many times have I waited for the spectacular when He asked only for trust?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Naaman's anger shows us the wall between him and healing: his pride. He expected Elisha to come out, to perform, to honor his rank. He cannot imagine that God's power works through simple obedience, not showmanship. We all know this anger—the moment the Lord asks us to do what seems too small.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rivers of Damascus are closer, more impressive, easier. Naaman argues with the proposal as though reason were enough to heal leprosy. His wisdom says no, his dignity says no, his comfort says no. He turns away in a rage—and almost loses everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His servants speak what he needs to hear: If he would do a great and difficult thing, why not this simple one? There's wisdom in their words—the humility to be taught by those who serve us. Naaman hears them. And he listens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He goes down into the Jordan seven times. Each dipping is an act of surrender, a death and rising again. On the seventh time his flesh returns—clean as a child's. The Lord meets him not at the point of his strength but at the point of his obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Naaman's eyes are opened. He sees that the God of Israel alone is God—not one god among many, but the only God. His healing brings him not just to clean skin but to the knowledge of the Lord. He stands before Elisha a new man, ready to give everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha refuses the gift. "As Yahweh lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none." A prophet doesn't do God's work for payment. His standing before the Lord is his wealth. I've noticed how the closest servants of the Lord often give away what the world prizes most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Naaman asks for earth—two mules' burden—to take back to Syria. He will worship the Lord only, make no more offerings to other gods. The earth of Israel means something sacred to him now. He carries a piece of the land where the true God is known.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But he asks for mercy in one thing—when his master bows in Rimmon's house and Naaman must support him, he asks the Lord to pardon him. It's a prayer of a man caught between his new faith and his duty. The Lord's grace meets him there too, in that complicated middle place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Go in peace." Elisha's blessing releases Naaman into his new life. The prophet speaks not judgment but peace—peace with his past, peace with his future, peace with his God. A simple word of grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gehazi sees Naaman departing with all his gifts still in hand—and greed awakens. His master refused payment out of faithfulness to the Lord, but Gehazi sees only wealth left behind. It's the beginning of a fall that will follow swift and terrible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gehazi runs after Naaman with a lie ready on his tongue. Naaman, honored and grateful, welcomes him from his chariot. A servant's deception is about to meet a prophet's sight. The Lord knows what is hidden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lie unfolds smoothly: prophets have come from Ephraim, they need silver and clothing. It sounds reasonable, almost humble—just a small gift for the young prophets. But it builds on deception from the ground up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Naaman, grateful and generous, gives far more than asked—two talents instead of one. His joy in giving becomes the instrument of Gehazi's theft. Sometimes our generosity is tested by those who would abuse it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gehazi takes the silver, hides it in the house, and lets the servants go. He thinks no one saw. He thinks Elisha, back in the city, didn't see. But the Lord's prophet doesn't need his eyes to know what his heart sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gehazi stands before Elisha and lies to his face: "Your servant went nowhere." The deception is complete and, in his mind, undetectable. But Elisha's sight reaches farther than the roads of Damascus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Didn't my heart go with you?" Elisha speaks the truth plainly. He saw Gehazi turn from his chariot, saw the transaction, saw the greed. Is this the time to take money? The word strips away all pretense.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Naaman's leprosy passes to Gehazi—white as snow, it cleaves to him and his offspring forever. Readers today hear an echo: we reap what we sow, and sin's wages are paid not just in coin but in the death it brings to our soul. Elisha's final word is mercy wrapped in justice—the Lord's account is kept, His holiness upheld, His warnings heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
